title: The struggle to capture the Nuremberg Trials
gist: A review of Sylvie Lindeperg's 'Staging Nuremberg' argues the trials were as much a media-production problem as a legal one: control of cameras, film and photographs shaped how Nazi guilt was communicated to the world, with the Jackson-vs-Donovan and US-vs-Soviet fights over portrayal proving as consequential as the courtroom verdicts.

insights.claim: Sylvie Lindeperg's book 'Staging Nuremberg' argues the Nuremberg Trials were never just about establishing legal guilt but equally about the presentation and portrayal of the guilty to a global audience.
insights.speaker: Iain MacGregor
insights.so_what: Frames war-crimes and transitional-justice tribunals generally as communications operations as much as legal ones — a lens applicable to how modern international tribunals (e.g. ICC proceedings) manage media and public perception today.
insights.quote: Nuremberg was never simply about establishing guilt but also about the presentation of the guilty and the portrayal of their crimes.

insights.claim: US press officer Gordon Dean wrote in 1945 that 'the world must be convinced that we are right' and that if the publicity campaign around the trials failed, it would have been better to hold no trials at all.
insights.speaker: Iain MacGregor
insights.so_what: Illustrates how early post-war US strategists treated legitimacy-signaling as a precondition for the legal process itself — a framework relevant to any state actor running high-stakes public tribunals or truth commissions.
insights.quote: The world must be convinced that we are right… If such a campaign fails it would be better that there be no trials.
insights.locator: Gordon Dean, 1945, quoted at top of review

insights.claim: The Allies made an unprecedented decision to let cameras into the Nuremberg courtroom specifically so they could frame the Nazi regime as a legally, proportionately punished perpetrator of crimes against humanity rather than merely a defeated military foe.
insights.speaker: Iain MacGregor
insights.so_what: Shows a deliberate causal chain: camera access -> perceived legitimacy -> durable historical narrative — a template for how visibility choices shape the long-run legacy of legal proceedings.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning 'The problem facing the Allies in 1945'

themes.theme: Jackson vs. Donovan: evidence vs. theatre

insights.claim: Robert Jackson, who led the US prosecution, wanted to build the case through documents, memoranda and captured archives, while William 'Wild Bill' Donovan (OSS chief, forerunner of the CIA) wanted a more theatrical prosecution built on witnesses, stories and emotional impact; Jackson's approach ultimately won out.
insights.speaker: Iain MacGregor
insights.so_what: A reusable framework for weighing 'documentary/evidentiary' versus 'narrative/theatrical' legitimation strategies in any public accountability process — evidentiary approaches produce durable authority but risk losing the audience.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning 'Nuremberg was constantly balancing two competing demands'

insights.claim: The prosecution's reliance on documentary evidence gave the Nuremberg tribunal its enduring historical authority, but also produced long stretches of courtroom tedium that caused journalists to complain and public attention to wander at the time.
insights.speaker: Iain MacGregor
insights.so_what: A trade-off worth generalizing: evidence-heavy legal processes buy long-term credibility at the cost of short-term public engagement — relevant to designing any high-visibility accountability proceeding today.

insights.claim: The reviewer argues that had Nuremberg placed greater emphasis on theatricality (Donovan's approach) and less on documentary evidence, the trial might have generated better contemporary headlines but left a weaker historical legacy.
insights.speaker: Iain MacGregor
insights.so_what: Pushes back against the book's apparent sympathy for Donovan, arguing durable institutional legitimacy should be prioritized over immediate media reception.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning 'I found myself occasionally resisting her conclusions'

themes.theme: Goering's performance and the limits of propaganda control

insights.claim: Hermann Goering understood courtroom performance instinctively and appeared energised rather than chastened by footage of Nazi atrocities screened as evidence, using his platform to appeal to an audience far beyond the courtroom.
insights.speaker: Iain MacGregor
insights.so_what: A cautionary case study: giving a defendant a public platform for 'evidence' can backfire if the defendant is media-savvy enough to reframe the spectacle to his own advantage.
insights.locator: paragraph on the screening of Nazi concentration-camp footage

insights.claim: One of the book's recurring lessons is that propaganda does not stop working simply because it is being played out in the ostensibly sober, neutral setting of a courtroom.
insights.speaker: Iain MacGregor
insights.so_what: A durable mental model for evaluating any 'neutral' institutional venue (courts, hearings, regulatory tribunals): formal neutrality of setting doesn't guarantee neutral reception of the content presented in it.
insights.quote: propaganda does not necessarily stop working simply because it is being played out in the apparently sober atmosphere of a courtroom.
insights.locator: paragraph on the screening of atrocity footage

insights.claim: The book's most original section concerns the Soviet role: Soviet filmmakers such as Roman Karmen produced clearer and more compelling cinematic interpretations of Nuremberg than the Americans, who were entangled in bureaucracy and competing agendas.
insights.speaker: Iain MacGregor
insights.so_what: Challenges the US-centric popular memory of Nuremberg, suggesting Soviet state media apparatus was operationally more effective at message discipline and speed than the American system at the time.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning 'The most original section of the book'

insights.claim: Budd Schulberg, later the Oscar-winning screenwriter of 'On the Waterfront', worked as a young US intelligence officer and film specialist tasked with hunting down hidden archives and surviving footage of Nazi crimes in defeated Germany.
insights.speaker: Iain MacGregor
insights.so_what: Illustrates that the survival of key visual evidence of the Third Reich's crimes was contingent and effortful, not an inevitable historical outcome.
